y-m-26-01.title: If you know two sides and one angle, is the triangle determined as one?
y-m-26-01.topic: Congruence conditions of triangles (two sides and one angle)
y-m-26-01.goal: Show by making counterexamples yourself that the claim 'two sides and one angle are equal' may not hold depending on where the angle is, and judge what more is needed to be sure the triangles are congruent.
y-m-26-01.material:
Jihu said, "In triangle ABC and triangle DEF, if AC=DF=10cm, BC=EF=6.5cm, and ∠A=∠D, then the two triangles are congruent!"

So that we can test it, I placed triangle ABC on the coordinate plane (one square is 1cm). A is the origin (0, 0) and C is (8, 6). Then AC=10cm. B is a point on the x-axis, to the right of A (its x-coordinate is positive). ∠A is the angle formed by segment AB on the x-axis and segment AC. We can place triangle DEF in the same way so that AC=DF and ∠A=∠D. Now find the point B with BC=6.5cm.
y-m-26-01.thinking.0: Reading the condition of the claim (where is the angle?)
y-m-26-01.thinking.2: Judging whether the information is sufficient and finding what more is needed
y-m-26-01.prereq.0: Having learned the congruence conditions of triangles SSS, SAS, ASA (grade 8 level)
y-m-26-01.prereq.1: The position of points on the coordinate plane and the distance between two points
y-m-26-01.prereq.2: Relationships among the three sides of a right triangle (helpful when checking lengths)
y-m-26-01.s.s1.prompt: What do you think of Jihu's claim? Choose the most reasonable judgment right now.
y-m-26-01.s.s1.hint.0: In Jihu's conditions, write down the names of the two sides whose lengths are given and the names of the two sides that form ∠A.
y-m-26-01.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the two lists and check whether ∠A is between the two given sides.
y-m-26-01.s.s1.o.a: They are congruent. Two sides and one angle are equal, so it falls under the SAS congruence condition
y-m-26-01.s.s1.r.a: SAS is used only when the angles between the two sides are equal. In this problem, ∠A is the angle between which two of the sides AC and BC?
y-m-26-01.s.s1.o.b: It may differ depending on where the angle is. Draw it to see if there is another triangle
y-m-26-01.s.s1.r.b: This is an attitude that also thinks about the position of the angle and tries to check the judgment with a test.
y-m-26-01.s.s1.o.c: They are not congruent. Two sides and one angle can never determine a triangle
y-m-26-01.s.s1.r.c: It is a problem to generalize with 'never'. When two sides and the angle between them are given, the triangle is determined (SAS). Think about where the angle is.
y-m-26-01.s.s1.o.d: Before seeing a picture, I cannot say anything about whether they are congruent or not
y-m-26-01.s.s1.r.d: The conditions are given as numbers, so you can test them even without a picture. Make them yourself with coordinates or a sketch.
y-m-26-01.s.s1.explain: Jihu shortened the condition to 'two sides and one angle'. In this problem, ∠A is not the angle between the given two sides AC and BC. The result can differ depending on where the angle is, so let's test it yourself in the next step.
y-m-26-01.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 different triangles ABC that satisfy all of Jihu's conditions. You only need to decide the x-coordinate bx of point B. (B is on the x-axis.)
y-m-26-01.s.s2.hint.0: Let point B be (b, 0), and write in words the condition on b so that the distance to C(8, 6) is 6.5.
y-m-26-01.s.s2.hint.1: Work out how far horizontally B must be from the point (8, 0), where the perpendicular from C meets the x-axis, and look at both the left and the right of that point.
y-m-26-01.s.s2.ok.c1: B is on the x-axis to the right of A.
y-m-26-01.s.s2.fail.c1: B must be to the right of A(0, 0), that is, a point on the x-axis whose x-coordinate is greater than 0.
y-m-26-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The length of BC is not 6.5cm. Check the distance between point B and C(8, 6) again.
y-m-26-01.s.s2.explain: If B=(5.5, 0), then AB=5.5cm, and if B=(10.5, 0), then AB=10.5cm. In both triangles AC=10cm, BC=6.5cm, and ∠A is also the same, but AB differs so they are not congruent. Jihu's claim has a counterexample, this case, where it does not hold.
y-m-26-01.s.s3.prompt: Now you want to sort out whether the two triangles are congruent. What is already known is AC=DF=10cm, BC=EF=6.5cm, ∠A=∠D. Choose all the options that, when just one of the following is also made known on top of this, let you be sure the triangles are congruent.
y-m-26-01.s.s3.hint.0: For the two triangles you made above (AB=5.5 and AB=10.5), work out for each whether the value in the option is different or the same.
y-m-26-01.s.s3.hint.1: If the value in the option comes out the same in both triangles, that information cannot tell them apart. Find the value that comes out different.
y-m-26-01.s.s3.o.a: The length of the perpendicular from C to AB (or its extension) is 6cm in both triangles
y-m-26-01.s.s3.r.a: This value is already fixed by AC=10 and ∠A alone. It is not new information, so it cannot separate the two cases.
y-m-26-01.s.s3.o.b: The lengths of AB and DE are equal
y-m-26-01.s.s3.o.c: ∠B and ∠E are both not right angles
y-m-26-01.s.s3.r.c: 'Not a right angle' applies to both cases. It cannot be information that separates the two cases.
y-m-26-01.s.s3.o.d: The perimeters of the two triangles are equal
y-m-26-01.s.s3.o.e: The sizes of ∠C and ∠F are equal
y-m-26-01.s.s3.explain: If AB is the same, all three sides are the same (SSS). If the perimeters are equal, then removing the already equal AC and BC leaves AB equal. ∠C is the angle between AC and BC, so two sides and their included angle become equal (SAS). On the other hand, the perpendicular length of 6cm or 'not a right angle' already applies to both triangles, so they cannot tell them apart.

y-m-26-02.title: Where is the problem in this proof?
y-m-26-02.topic: Properties of isosceles triangles and errors in a proof
y-m-26-02.goal: Find the error of using the conclusion to be shown as evidence in a proof, and judge that it can be fixed in different ways so that the congruence condition holds correctly.
y-m-26-02.material: Seohyeon wants to prove 'In triangle ABC, if AB = AC, then ∠B = ∠C'. AB = AC is the assumption and ∠B = ∠C is the conclusion to be proved. Below is the proof Seohyeon wrote. Read it while telling the assumption and the conclusion apart. Point M is a point on side BC. (There is no figure. Imagine triangle ABC with a segment drawn from vertex A down to side BC.)
y-m-26-02.thinking.0: Splitting the lines of a proof into assumption/conclusion to find the error
y-m-26-02.thinking.1: Comparing several correct ways to fix it
y-m-26-02.thinking.2: Explaining the reason for the error in writing
y-m-26-02.prereq.0: The meaning of an isosceles triangle (a triangle with two sides of equal length)
y-m-26-02.prereq.1: Triangle congruence conditions SSS, SAS, and the right-triangle congruence condition RHS
y-m-26-02.s.s1.prompt: Seohyeon wrote the following, saying she proves 'the two base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal in size'. Choose the line that is hard to accept as a proof.
y-m-26-02.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, mark whether it uses 'what is given (the assumption)' or 'what is to be shown (the conclusion)'.
y-m-26-02.s.s1.hint.1: Sort the three things in line 3 into whether each is an assumption, something obtained in a previous line, or what was to be proved.
y-m-26-02.s.s1.line.0: In triangle ABC, AB = AC. (To show: ∠B = ∠C)
y-m-26-02.s.s1.line.1: Let M be the midpoint of side BC and connect A and M with a segment. Then BM = CM.
y-m-26-02.s.s1.line.2: In triangle ABM and triangle ACM, AB = AC, ∠B = ∠C (base angles of an isosceles triangle), and AM is common.
y-m-26-02.s.s1.line.3: Therefore triangle ABM and triangle ACM are congruent.
y-m-26-02.s.s1.line.4: In congruent triangles the corresponding angles are equal in size, so ∠B = ∠C.
y-m-26-02.s.s1.explain: In line 3, ∠B = ∠C was already written as if it were a fact. That is the conclusion the proof is meant to show. As a result, the congruence in line 4 has no basis either (AB, ∠B, AM are not two sides and the included angle), and line 5 ends up concluding by repeating what was written at the start.
y-m-26-02.s.s2.prompt: You want to fix Seohyeon's proof. When changing the way of showing congruence in line 3, choose all the ways that make the proof correct.
y-m-26-02.s.s2.hint.0: For each way, check whether the three things used are all assumptions, or follow directly from how point M is chosen.
y-m-26-02.s.s2.hint.1: Compare whether it has the form that matches a congruence condition (SSS, SAS, RHS). Also check whether any option uses the conclusion ∠B = ∠C.
y-m-26-02.s.s2.o.a: Take M as the foot of the perpendicular from A to BC and compare using AB = AC, AM common, ∠AMB = ∠AMC = 90°
y-m-26-02.s.s2.o.b: Write ∠B = ∠C and add that this is right because it looks that way in the figure
y-m-26-02.s.s2.r.b: Looking that way in the figure is not a basis for a proof. A proof shows the reason why it looks that way.
y-m-26-02.s.s2.o.c: Take M as the point where the bisector of ∠A meets BC and compare using AB = AC, ∠BAM = ∠CAM, AM common
y-m-26-02.s.s2.o.d: Write that triangles ABM and ACM are congruent because their areas are equal, and then write that the corresponding angles are equal
y-m-26-02.s.s2.r.d: Even if the areas are equal, the shapes can differ (for example, rectangles with different widths and heights). Equal area alone does not make them congruent.
y-m-26-02.s.s2.o.e: Take M as the midpoint of BC and compare using AB = AC, BM = CM, AM common
y-m-26-02.s.s2.explain: e is congruent because the three sides are equal (SSS), c because two sides and the included angle are equal (SAS), and a because the hypotenuse and one other side of a right triangle are equal (RHS). None of the ways writes ∠B = ∠C in advance; they get ∠B = ∠C from the congruence.
y-m-26-02.s.s3.prompt: Write a message to tell Seohyeon. Say why the original proof cannot be said to have shown 'the base angles are equal', and write how to fix it with one of the ways above.
y-m-26-02.s.s3.hint.0: First write in one sentence which of the three things written in line 3 is what is to be proved.
y-m-26-02.s.s3.hint.1: Choose a way you like from the options above, write down the three things it uses, and check whether they match the name of a congruence condition.
y-m-26-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: In your writing, is it clear 'what was already used in which line'?
y-m-26-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: In the way you fixed it, are you using ∠B = ∠C only as the conclusion?
y-m-26-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: In the way you fixed it, are all three things of the congruence condition given, or do they come from how point M was chosen?
y-m-26-02.s.s3.model.0: Line 3 already uses ∠B = ∠C. That is the conclusion to be proved, so it must not be used as a basis. You can fix it by using SSS congruence with the assumption AB = AC, BM = CM that arises because M is the midpoint, and the common AM.
y-m-26-02.s.s3.model.1: It brings in ∠B = ∠C, which is to be shown, as the basis for congruence first, so the proof goes in circles. If you take point M using the bisector of ∠A and use SAS congruence with AB = AC, ∠BAM = ∠CAM, AM common, you do not have to assume ∠B = ∠C in advance.

y-m-26-03.title: What changes as more is known about the diagonals?
y-m-26-03.topic: Properties of the diagonals of quadrilaterals, and identifying quadrilaterals
y-m-26-03.goal: Explain, connecting to the conditions, how the judgment that a quadrilateral is a rectangle or a square changes as information about the diagonals is added one piece at a time, and confirm with examples you make yourself that the first information alone is not enough.
y-m-26-03.material: The two diagonals of quadrilateral ABCD are AC and BD. A rectangle is a quadrilateral whose four angles are all right angles, a rhombus is a quadrilateral whose four sides all have the same length, and a square is a quadrilateral whose four angles are all right angles and whose four sides all have the same length. Suppose you already know that 'a quadrilateral whose two diagonals bisect each other is a parallelogram'. All the quadrilaterals are considered to be convex quadrilaterals (quadrilaterals with no part dented inward).
y-m-26-03.thinking.0: Judging from partial information and revising when new information arrives
y-m-26-03.thinking.1: Working out whether the converse (the reverse) holds
y-m-26-03.prereq.0: The meaning of parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus, and square, and the properties of their diagonals (grade 8 level)
y-m-26-03.prereq.1: Among the conditions for a parallelogram, 'the two diagonals bisect each other'
y-m-26-03.prereq.2: The distance between two points on the coordinate plane
y-m-26-03.s.s1.prompt: For quadrilateral ABCD, information about the diagonals AC and BD is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, judge 'whether it can be said to be a rectangle'. (There is no figure.)
y-m-26-03.s.s1.hint.0: Rewrite each piece of information as a property of the 'diagonals' of the quadrilateral and compare it with the diagonal properties of a rectangle, a parallelogram, and a rhombus.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.hint.1: After gathering all the information known so far, draw to check whether a quadrilateral that satisfies all that information and is not a rectangle is possible.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.0.info: The two diagonals have the same length. (AC = BD)
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: Can quadrilateral ABCD be said to be a rectangle?
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.0.after: Among quadrilaterals with equal diagonals there are some that are not rectangles (for example, a trapezoid whose two legs have the same length). So this information alone cannot make you sure it is a rectangle. Look at the next information and revise your judgment.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It is a rectangle. Because a rectangle has diagonals of the same length
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: 'If it is a rectangle, the diagonals are equal' and 'if the diagonals are equal, it is a rectangle' go in different directions. Whether the reverse also holds has to be worked out separately.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: You cannot assert it is a rectangle. There seem to be quadrilaterals that are not rectangles even if the diagonals are equal
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You can draw a quadrilateral that has only the diagonal lengths equal. If there is even one, you cannot assert it.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is not a rectangle. Because nothing says they bisect each other
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: It might be a rectangle. 'Nothing says they bisect each other' and 'they do not bisect each other' are different.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.0.o.d: The information is lacking, so we cannot tell now. It might or might not be a rectangle
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.1.info: New knowledge: the two diagonals bisect each other. (If the intersection of the diagonals is O, then AO = CO, BO = DO) The earlier information (AC = BD) is still the case.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: Can quadrilateral ABCD now be said to be a rectangle?
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.1.after: If the diagonals bisect each other, it is a parallelogram. In parallelogram ABCD, comparing triangle ABD and triangle DCA, AB = DC, AD = DA (common), BD = CA, so they are congruent (SSS), and ∠A = ∠D. Since AB ∥ DC, ∠A + ∠D = 180°, so ∠A = ∠D = 90°. Therefore it is a rectangle.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: We can only know it is a parallelogram and still do not know whether it is a rectangle
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: It is right that it is a parallelogram. But you can keep using the 'AC = BD' you knew at the start. What changes when you use the two pieces of information together?
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It is not a rectangle but a rhombus
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: For a rhombus you need the information that the four sides are equal. So far there is no information about the side lengths.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It is a rectangle. It is a parallelogram whose two diagonals have the same length, so the four angles become equal
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.1.o.d: It is a square. Because the diagonals bisect each other
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: To be a square, you need the further information that the four sides are equal. Bisecting alone tells you only up to a parallelogram.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.2.info: Last thing learned: the two diagonals meet perpendicularly. (AC ⊥ BD)
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: Combining it with all the earlier information, what is the most detailed name for ABCD?
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.2.after: In a quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect each other, if the diagonals are perpendicular, it is a rhombus (four equal sides). It was already a rectangle, so all four angles are right angles and all four sides are equal, so it is a square. The 'rectangle' from the earlier step is still correct, but the new information made the name more specific.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Rhombus is not a wrong word either (they bisect each other and are perpendicular). But if you also combine the information from the earlier step that it is a rectangle, there is a more detailed name.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Saying rectangle is not wrong. But you did not use the 'perpendicular' that was newly found this time. What is a parallelogram with perpendicular diagonals?
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.2.o.d: It is a parallelogram but not a rectangle
y-m-26-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You learned in the earlier step that it is a rectangle. New information cannot overturn an earlier conclusion.
y-m-26-03.s.s1.reflect: Think about why the first information (equal diagonal lengths) alone could not make you sure it is a rectangle, what the second piece of information added, and whether the last piece of information changed or added to the earlier conclusion.
y-m-26-03.s.s2.prompt: Let's check for ourselves that when only the first information (AC = BD) is known, it might not be a rectangle. Place A(0, 0) and B(6, 0), and make 2 different convex quadrilaterals ABCD whose diagonals AC and BD have the same length and which are not parallelograms. (The coordinates of points C and D)
y-m-26-03.s.s2.hint.0: Fix one point C and look for where a point D could be whose distance from B equals 'the distance from A to C'.
y-m-26-03.s.s2.hint.1: Draw the quadrilateral with the points you chose and also check whether sides AB and DC are parallel and whether sides AD and BC are parallel.
y-m-26-03.s.s2.ok.c1: C and D are above side AB.
y-m-26-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The y-coordinates of C and D must be greater than 0 (above AB).
y-m-26-03.s.s2.ok.c2: It is a convex quadrilateral connecting A, B, C, D in order.
y-m-26-03.s.s2.fail.c2: If you connect A, B, C, D in order, it is a quadrilateral that is concave or crossing over itself. Choose the points again so that it becomes a quadrilateral whose four angles are all less than 180°.
y-m-26-03.s.s2.ok.c3: The two diagonals have the same length.
y-m-26-03.s.s2.fail.c3: The lengths of AC and BD are not equal. Calculate the lengths of the two diagonals separately and compare them.
y-m-26-03.s.s2.fail.c4: This quadrilateral is a parallelogram (including a rectangle). Make an example that is not a parallelogram.
y-m-26-03.s.s2.explain: For example, if C(5, 3) and D(1, 3), then AC² = 34 and BD² = 25 + 9 = 34 (a trapezoid whose two legs have the same length). If C(4, 3) and D(3, 4), then AC = BD = 5 but no two sides are parallel. Both have equal diagonals but are not rectangles. So you cannot be sure from the diagonal lengths alone.

y-m-26-04.title: What do we need to know to find the width of the pond?
y-m-26-04.topic: The segment connecting the midpoints of two sides of a triangle
y-m-26-04.goal: Distinguish by piece of information the conditions under which the midpoint theorem holds, explain by making a situation why parallelism alone cannot determine the length, and choose an attitude for handling the difference between theoretical and measured values.
y-m-26-04.material: There are points B and C on the edge of a pond, so BC cannot be measured directly. A point A is chosen outside the pond, a rope is pulled taut, point M is set on segment AB and point N on segment AC, and only MN was measured and came out to 30m. All the points are on the same flat ground. The students claimed 'BC = 60m'. In the first two steps, assume there is no measurement error in the tape measure.
y-m-26-04.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient
y-m-26-04.thinking.1: Making a counterexample situation when only some of the conditions are present
y-m-26-04.thinking.2: Interpreting the difference between theoretical and measured values
y-m-26-04.prereq.0: The properties of the segment connecting the midpoints of two sides of a triangle (grade 8 level)
y-m-26-04.prereq.1: The meaning of similarity of triangles (similarity ratio)
y-m-26-04.prereq.2: Ratios of segment lengths and parallel lines (helpful for understanding)
y-m-26-04.s.s1.prompt: B and C are the two ends of the pond, so BC cannot be measured directly. Point M is on AB, point N is on AC, and MN = 30m. The students claimed 'BC = 60m'. On top of this, when each of the following pieces of information is added 'one at a time', choose all those with which you can be sure that BC = 60m.
y-m-26-04.s.s1.hint.0: For each option, write in one line whether the positions of M on AB and N on AC are determined.
y-m-26-04.s.s1.hint.1: For an option in which the position of M or N is not determined, think about whether the ratio of BC to MN would change if you moved that point.
y-m-26-04.s.s1.r.a: If they are parallel and AM = AN, all you can know is that AB = AC. If you do not know where on AB M is, you cannot know how many times MN BC is.
y-m-26-04.s.s1.o.b: M is the midpoint of AB, and N is the midpoint of AC
y-m-26-04.s.s1.o.c: M is the midpoint of AB, and AM = AN
y-m-26-04.s.s1.r.c: Even if M is a midpoint, you cannot know whether N is the midpoint of AC. This is because AB and AC could be different.
y-m-26-04.s.s1.r.d: If they are merely parallel, a parallel segment comes out wherever you put M. The ratio of the lengths changes depending on the position of M.
y-m-26-04.s.s1.o.e: M is the midpoint of AB, and MN ∥ BC
y-m-26-04.s.s1.explain: The segment connecting the midpoints of two sides is parallel to the remaining side and half its length. Also, 'a line through the midpoint of one side and parallel to another side' passes through the midpoint of the remaining side too. So b and e guarantee BC = 2 × MN = 60m. For the rest, the position of M (or of N) is not determined, so BC might not be 60m.
y-m-26-04.s.s2.prompt: Think about the case where you only know option d (MN ∥ BC). Make a situation in which BC is not 60m, write the length of BC as a number, and explain why it comes out that way.
y-m-26-04.s.s2.hint.0: Keep MN ∥ BC as it is and think about what happens to the ratio of the lengths of segment MN and BC when you move point M along AB toward A or toward B.
y-m-26-04.s.s2.hint.1: Fix one M, write AM : AB concretely, and calculate BC from that ratio and MN = 30m.
y-m-26-04.s.s2.placeholder: Example: If M is at ... of AB, then ...
y-m-26-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Is the length of BC you wrote calculated correctly from the position of M (AM : AB) and MN = 30m?
y-m-26-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write that 'if they are merely parallel, M can be anywhere'?
y-m-26-04.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you compare it with the fact that it becomes 60m when M is the midpoint?
y-m-26-04.s.s2.model.0: Even if MN ∥ BC, it depends on the position of M. For example, if AM is one third of AB, the similarity ratio is 1 : 3, so BC is 3 times MN, that is, 90m. It is 60m only when M is the midpoint, so you cannot assert 60m from parallelism alone.
y-m-26-04.s.s2.model.1: Even if M is not the midpoint of AB but a point closer to B, you can still draw it with MN ∥ BC. If AM : AB is 3 : 4, then MN : BC is also 3 : 4, so BC is 40m. So you cannot be sure it is 60m from the information of parallelism alone.
y-m-26-04.s.s3.prompt: After confirming information b (M and N are each midpoints), you actually measured BC with the tape measure and got 58m (MN is 30m). Choose all the fitting attitudes toward handling this result.
y-m-26-04.s.s3.hint.0: Estimate what percent of the theoretical value the difference between the theoretical and measured values is.
y-m-26-04.s.s3.hint.1: Write down all the conditions that must be kept for the theorem to hold (positions of points, lengths) and think about where errors could arise on site.
y-m-26-04.s.s3.o.a: Recheck the midpoint marks and measure MN and BC once more
y-m-26-04.s.s3.o.b: Conclude that the midpoint theorem does not hold on real ground
y-m-26-04.s.s3.r.b: The theorem is about when the points are exact midpoints and the lengths are exact. In reality, errors arise in the midpoint marks and the tape measure.
y-m-26-04.s.s3.o.c: Regard 58m as wrong and use the theoretical value 60m as the correct answer
y-m-26-04.s.s3.r.c: If you ignore the measured value and trust only the theoretical value, you miss the possibility that the midpoint marks or the ground conditions were wrong. You must first check the difference between the two values.
y-m-26-04.s.s3.o.d: Work out whether a 2m difference is within what could come from the midpoint positions or the tape measure's error
y-m-26-04.s.s3.o.e: Rewrite MN as 29m so that BC is 58m and wrap it up that way
y-m-26-04.s.s3.r.e: You must not change a value to make it fit. You changed a number without checking which value had the error.
y-m-26-04.s.s3.explain: The 2m difference between the theoretical value 60m and the measured value 58m is a little over 3%. The midpoint marks may have been slightly off, the rope may not have been taut, or the ground may not have been flat. The fitting attitude is to measure again and work out the size of the error. You must not change the measured value or the theoretical value arbitrarily.

y-m-26-05.title: Can we make triangles of area 12 in many ways?
y-m-26-05.topic: The area of triangles between parallel lines
y-m-26-05.goal: Understand that the condition for triangles with the same base to have the same area is the height, and find several points that satisfy the area and angle-size conditions at the same time, explaining the reason.
y-m-26-05.material: On the coordinate plane, let the length of one square be 1cm. There are points A(0, 0) and B(6, 0), and point P is above the x-axis. You look for a point P such that the area of triangle ABP is 12cm², and the coordinates of P are integers.
y-m-26-05.thinking.0: Finding several solutions that satisfy constraints at the same time
y-m-26-05.thinking.1: Grasping the place (shape) where the points lie
y-m-26-05.thinking.2: Explaining why the areas are the same
y-m-26-05.prereq.0: Area of a triangle = base × height ÷ 2 (grade 5 elementary level)
y-m-26-05.prereq.1: The position of points on the coordinate plane, and the meaning of acute, right, and obtuse angles
y-m-26-05.prereq.2: If two lines are parallel, the distance between them is constant (distance between parallel lines)
y-m-26-05.s.s1.prompt: On the coordinate plane there are A(0, 0) and B(6, 0). You want point P to be above the x-axis and the area of triangle ABP to be 12cm². What shape would you get if you gathered all such points P? (One square is 1cm)
y-m-26-05.s.s1.hint.0: Think about how tall the height must be for the area to be 12 when you view AB as the base of triangle ABP.
y-m-26-05.s.s1.hint.1: When you move P up and down perpendicular to AB, think about the directions in which you can move while keeping the same height.
y-m-26-05.s.s1.o.a: Points on a circle at a constant distance from A
y-m-26-05.s.s1.r.a: Even if points on a circle are at the same distance from A, their distance from AB (the height) varies.
y-m-26-05.s.s1.o.b: Only one point. Once the area is fixed at 12, P is fixed as one
y-m-26-05.s.s1.r.b: Having the same base and the same area means having the same height. Is there only one point with the same height?
y-m-26-05.s.s1.o.c: Points on the line that passes through the middle of AB and is perpendicular to AB
y-m-26-05.s.s1.r.c: The points on this line have different distances from AB, so the heights vary. The areas become different from each other.
y-m-26-05.s.s1.o.d: Points on the line that is parallel to AB and 4cm away from AB
y-m-26-05.s.s1.explain: The base AB = 6cm is the same, so for the area to be 12cm², the height must be 12 × 2 ÷ 6 = 4cm. The points at height 4cm from AB are all the points on the line parallel to AB (y = 4).
y-m-26-05.s.s2.prompt: Find 3 different points P such that the area of triangle ABP is 12cm² and all three angles are acute (angles smaller than 90°). The coordinates of P are integers.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.hint.0: Among the points on the line you found in the previous step, change the x-coordinate one at a time and check whether the angles are acute.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.hint.1: Draw what happens to the angles at points A and B when the x-coordinate is too small or too large.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.ok.c1: P is a point with integer coordinates above the x-axis.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.fail.c1: P must be above the x-axis (y>0) and have integer coordinates.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.ok.c2: The area of triangle ABP is 12.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.fail.c2: The area of triangle ABP is not 12cm². Check the base AB and the height again.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.fail.c3: One of the three angles is a right angle or an obtuse angle. Check the angles at points A, B, and P one by one.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.explain: If P is (1, 4), (2, 4), (3, 4), (4, 4), (5, 4), all have height 4cm so the area is 12. If the x-coordinate is 0 or 6, there is a right angle at A or B, and outside of that it is obtuse. So these five are the only integer points. The point (3, 4) gives an isosceles triangle, and the rest are triangles of various shapes.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.because.prompt: Compare the points you found. Explain why the areas are the same even though the shape of the triangle differs for each point, and how the acute-angle condition limited the positions of the points.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: Compare the y-coordinates of the points you found and say what line they lie on.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: Draw how many degrees the angles at points A and B are when the x-coordinate of P is 0 and when it is 6.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you explain why the areas are the same as 'the base is the same and the height is the same too'?
y-m-26-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you explain with angles why it does not work if the x-coordinate is 0, 6, or outside?
y-m-26-05.s.s2.because.model.0: The points are on a line parallel to AB, so viewing AB as the base, the heights are all the same 4, and the base is the same 6, so the areas are all 12. If the x-coordinate is 0 or 6, there is a right angle at A or B, and if it is less than 0 or more than 6 it is obtuse, so only 1 to 5 work.
y-m-26-05.s.s2.because.model.1: The base AB is 6 and the height is the same 4, so even if the shapes differ the areas are the same. The angles have to be acute, so P must not be directly above A or B or outside them, and the x-coordinate must be between 0 and 6.

y-m-26-06.title: How can we fill the space around a point by mixing regular polygons?
y-m-26-06.topic: Interior angles of regular polygons and the angles around a point
y-m-26-06.goal: Connect one interior angle of a regular polygon with the 360° of the angles around a point to find several combinations that fit the condition, and explain how to find them without missing any and that this condition concerns a single vertex.
y-m-26-06.material: A tile workshop wants to use equilateral triangle, square, and regular hexagon tiles. All the tiles have the same side length, so they can be joined exactly side to side. In this task, you only work out whether, when several tiles are gathered at one vertex, the angles around that point make exactly 360° with no gaps and no overlaps. Whether this can cover the whole plane is not dealt with.
y-m-26-06.thinking.1: Designing a systematic way to find them without missing any
y-m-26-06.thinking.2: Telling necessary conditions apart from sufficient conditions
y-m-26-06.prereq.0: The sum of the interior angles of a polygon and one interior angle of a regular n-gon (grade 8 level)
y-m-26-06.prereq.1: The angles around a point total 360°
y-m-26-06.prereq.2: The relationship between divisors and multiples (dividing evenly)
y-m-26-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the regular polygons for which several copies of that one kind alone can exactly fill the space around a point with no gaps and no overlaps. (One interior angle of a regular n-gon is 180° × (n − 2) ÷ n.)
y-m-26-06.s.s1.hint.0: Find one interior angle of each regular polygon with the formula and write it in a table.
y-m-26-06.s.s1.hint.1: Check how many times each interior angle must be added to make exactly 360°, and see whether there is a remainder.
y-m-26-06.s.s1.r.a: One interior angle is 135°; check what happens when you divide 360° by 135°.
y-m-26-06.s.s1.r.d: One interior angle is 108°; check whether 360° is divisible by 108°.
y-m-26-06.s.s1.explain: The angles around a point are 360°. If one interior angle is 60°, 90°, or 120°, exactly 6, 4, or 3 of them fill it. 108° and 135° do not divide 360° evenly. Gaps appear or they overlap.
y-m-26-06.s.s2.prompt: This time you may mix equilateral triangles, squares, and regular hexagons. Make 3 different combinations that exactly fill the space around a point with no gaps and no overlaps, using two or more kinds among squares, equilateral triangles, and regular hexagons. (The number of each shape)
y-m-26-06.s.s2.hint.0: Try the numbers of each shape whose interior angles add up to 360°. It is good to decide the number of one kind first.
y-m-26-06.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate the sum with the numbers you chose; if it falls short of 360°, add shapes, and if it goes over, change the shapes.
y-m-26-06.s.s2.ok.c1: The numbers are integers that are 0 or more.
y-m-26-06.s.s2.fail.c1: The numbers must be integers that are 0 or more.
y-m-26-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The sum of the angles is exactly 360°.
y-m-26-06.s.s2.fail.c2: The sum of the angles is not 360°. Add 60° for an equilateral triangle, 90° for a square, and 120° for a regular hexagon as many times as the number of each.
y-m-26-06.s.s2.ok.c3: You mixed two or more kinds.
y-m-26-06.s.s2.fail.c3: This is a combination using only one kind. Mix two or more kinds.
y-m-26-06.s.s2.explain: The integer combinations that exactly fill the space around a point with two or more of equilateral triangles, squares, and regular hexagons are only the four (equilateral triangles, squares, regular hexagons) = (3, 2, 0), (1, 2, 1), (4, 0, 1), (2, 0, 2). However, the sum being 360° at one point is only one necessary condition, and whether this way can actually cover the whole plane requires checking the other vertices too.
y-m-26-06.s.s2.because.prompt: How should you search to be sure you have 'found all' such combinations? Write the method you will use.
y-m-26-06.s.s2.because.hint.0: Organize the combinations you have found so far in a table and look at in what order you found them.
y-m-26-06.s.s2.because.hint.1: Try the method of fixing the number of regular hexagons, like 0 and 1, and filling the remaining angle.
y-m-26-06.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: First decide the number of ... and ...
y-m-26-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Is the order clear in which you fix the number of one shape and work out the rest?
y-m-26-06.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write how you can know there are no more when you do it that way?
y-m-26-06.s.s2.because.model.0: If you set the number of regular hexagons in turn to 0, 1, 2, 3 and work out one by one whether the remaining angle can be filled with equilateral triangles of 60° and squares of 90°, you can find them without missing any. The sum is 360°, so there cannot be more than 3 regular hexagons.
y-m-26-06.s.s2.because.model.1: If you group the sum of 360° into units of 30°, an equilateral triangle is 2 units, a square is 3 units, and a regular hexagon is 4 units, so (number of equilateral triangles)×2+(number of squares)×3+(number of regular hexagons)×4=12. If you make a table and put the numbers in one by one, you can check every case.
y-m-26-06.s.s2.because.model.2: Fix the number of regular hexagons one at a time as 0, 1, 2, 3, and in order work out whether the remaining angle can be filled with regular triangles and squares, and organize all the cases in a table.

y-m-26-07.title: Is the circumcenter always inside the triangle?
y-m-26-07.topic: The position of a triangle's circumcenter
y-m-26-07.goal: Evaluate 'the circumcenter is always inside the triangle' with data from a table, make a prediction for a new triangle, and then state the position of the circumcenter by type of triangle, with conditions.
y-m-26-07.material:
The circumcenter of a triangle is the point at the same distance from the three vertices. Ara said, 'The circumcenter of a triangle is always inside the triangle.' Below are the results of investigating 5 triangles on the coordinate plane. (One square of the coordinates = 1cm. The coordinates of the circumcenter are values found by calculation.)

No. | Vertices A, B, C | Largest angle | Coordinates of the circumcenter | Position of the circumcenter
1 | (0,0), (6,0), (3,4) | about 74° | (3, 0.875) | inside the triangle
2 | (0,0), (8,0), (0,6) | 90° | (4, 3) | on side BC (midpoint of BC)
3 | (0,0), (10,0), (5,2) | about 136° | (5, −5.25) | outside the triangle
4 | (0,0), (7,0), (2,5) | about 68° | (3.5, 1.5) | inside the triangle
5 | (0,0), (5,0), (−1,2) | about 117° | (2.5, 2.5) | outside the triangle
y-m-26-07.thinking.2: Making a prediction from a table and recognizing the limits of generalization
y-m-26-07.prereq.0: The meaning of a triangle's circumcenter (the point at the same distance from the three vertices)
y-m-26-07.prereq.1: The meaning of acute, right, and obtuse triangles
y-m-26-07.prereq.2: Reading the position of points on the coordinate plane
y-m-26-07.s.s1.prompt: Ara said, 'The circumcenter of a triangle is always inside the triangle.' Choose everything that can be read from the table above alone.
y-m-26-07.s.s1.hint.0: Read the table line by line and mark whether the circumcenter is inside, on a side, or outside.
y-m-26-07.s.s1.hint.1: For each option, write which line numbers it is based on, and check that it really comes out that way on those lines.
y-m-26-07.s.s1.o.a: In rows 1 and 4 of the table, the circumcenter is inside the triangle
y-m-26-07.s.s1.o.b: Among the triangles in the table, only one has its circumcenter outside the triangle
y-m-26-07.s.s1.r.b: Count which numbers in the table are triangles with the circumcenter outside.
y-m-26-07.s.s1.o.c: I confirmed that the circumcenter is always on the longest side
y-m-26-07.s.s1.r.c: How many triangles in the table have the circumcenter on the longest side? Can one example let you say 'always'?
y-m-26-07.s.s1.o.d: Row 3 of the table is an example that does not fit Ara's statement
y-m-26-07.s.s1.o.e: Looking at the table alone, Ara's statement comes out right
y-m-26-07.s.s1.r.e: Check, in every row of the table, whether the circumcenter is inside.
y-m-26-07.s.s1.o.f: The table includes cases where the circumcenter is inside the triangle, on a side, and outside
y-m-26-07.s.s1.explain: In the table, rows 1 and 4 are inside, row 2 is on a side (midpoint of the hypotenuse), and rows 3 and 5 are outside. So examples like rows 3 and 5 do not fit 'always inside'. One or two examples cannot prove 'always', but one counterexample can break 'always'.
y-m-26-07.s.s2.prompt: There is a new triangle that is not in the table. Its vertices are A(0, 0), B(9, 0), C(4, 2). Before you have found the coordinates of the circumcenter, what would you do about the position of the circumcenter?
y-m-26-07.s.s2.hint.0: First compare the shapes of the triangles in the table whose circumcenter was outside (what their largest angle is like).
y-m-26-07.s.s2.hint.1: Draw where the vertex of the new triangle that is likely to have the largest angle is, and estimate whether it is greater than 90°.
y-m-26-07.s.s2.o.a: I predict it is inside the triangle. 2 of the 5 in the table were like that, so it is likely
y-m-26-07.s.s2.r.a: Only 2 of the 5 were inside. That too depended on the shape at the vertices; did you look at what shape this triangle has?
y-m-26-07.s.s2.o.b: I predict it is on side AB. Because the circumcenter is on the longest side
y-m-26-07.s.s2.r.b: What was special about the triangles in the table whose circumcenter was on a side? Check whether this triangle has that shape.
y-m-26-07.s.s2.o.c: It seems to be outside. Because it looks like it has a large angle, like rows 3 and 5 of the table
y-m-26-07.s.s2.o.d: I don't know until I calculate, and I'll find the coordinates of the circumcenter and check
y-m-26-07.s.s2.r.d: This is an attitude of putting off the prediction and checking directly. If you first make a prediction from the data in the table, you will know what to look at when you check.
y-m-26-07.s.s2.explain: C(4, 2) is marked low above the middle of A and B, so ∠C is obtuse (about 132°). It has a shape similar to row 3 of the table (an obtuse triangle). In fact the circumcenter is (4.5, −4), outside the triangle (below AB). It is fine to just predict without calculating, and checking by calculation is good too.
y-m-26-07.s.s2.acc.0: Putting off the prediction and calculating directly is also reasonable. But making a prediction from the data in the table and then checking by calculation is a better habit.
y-m-26-07.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite Ara's statement. Using the data in the table as evidence, write for what triangles the circumcenter is inside, on a side, and outside, and if there is a part not yet proved, say that too.
y-m-26-07.s.s3.hint.0: On each row of the table, write the type of the triangle (acute/right/obtuse) and the position of the circumcenter side by side.
y-m-26-07.s.s3.hint.1: Compare whether, when you group triangles of the same type, the position of the circumcenter has something in common.
y-m-26-07.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If all three angles are ...
y-m-26-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the rule you wrote fit all 5 triangle rows of the table?
y-m-26-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you give an example that breaks 'always'?
y-m-26-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say what part is not proved by the table alone?
y-m-26-07.s.s3.model.0: It seems that if all three angles are acute, the circumcenter is inside; if it is a right triangle, it is on the hypotenuse; and if it is an obtuse triangle, it is outside. The five triangles in the table were all like that, but I only looked at five, so I haven't proved it yet.
y-m-26-07.s.s3.model.1: 'Always inside' is wrong. Triangles with an obtuse angle, like rows 3 and 5 of the table, had the circumcenter outside, and the right triangle had it on a side. I want to calculate a few more new triangles to check.
